top.line: Allowed is not right: Northstar answered with three policies
top.para: Ashish Rajan's Northstar agent may refund $200; a customer owed $120 gets $150 and every control passes. His four questions are right. The behaviour policy answers SECURE, but VERIFY needs a written definition of right, a decision policy. A twin of his store shows what each design catches and what it costs.

in-short.line: SECURE is behaviour; VERIFY needs a decision policy
in-short.para: The $200 limit is a behaviour rule and it held. Proving the right outcome needs someone to have written down what right is. Mapped onto three policies and run as a twin: refusing is not being right, the right amount can come from the wrong decider, and the evidence for autonomy is the case record.

question.line: A refund allowed, logged and wrong
question.para: Northstar's agent may refund up to $200, enforced by the payment service. It misreads a discount and refunds $150 where $120 was owed. "The system did what it was allowed to do. It just didn't do what it was supposed to do." His answer is four connected questions: SECURE, OBSERVE, RESPOND and VERIFY.

secure.line: SECURE is what the behaviour policy already does
secure.para: An instruction not to exceed a limit is not a system enforcing it. The ABP's rows name a capability, reach and mandate, and say what keeps each: an expectation, a setting or a boundary. Northstar's $200 limit is such a row, enforced by the payment service, and it held.

verify.line: Proving right needs a written definition of right
verify.para: A limit cannot tell $150 from $120 when both are under $200. Verification needs an intended requirement: a rule for the amount and a decision about who works it out. That is a decision policy. The example also exposed a gap in my own series, now fixed with a fifth state, verified.

mapping.line: Four questions across three policies, every control placed
mapping.para: His questions cut across behaviour, decision and workflow. VERIFY has nothing in the behaviour column, because a limit only says what may be done. SECURE has a workflow cell: the agent proposes and the workflow pays, so a wrong proposal is a recorded difference, not a payment.

twin.line: The twin: refusing is not right, deciders matter
twin.para: Thirteen synthetic refunds through four designs. As described: $458 overpaid, $341.60 owed. Securing refuses and leaves customers waiting. Verifying gets every amount right at 57 minutes of people's time; three policies with precedents get every case right in 18, including a $261 refund split into three to dodge the limit.

second-model.line: Deterministic checks where rules exist; people for the rest
second-model.para: He warns a second model is not necessarily enough. The twin works out amounts with a calculator the agent cannot change, uses a person for cases with no rule, and records their decision with reasons so the next matching case needs neither.

five.line: His five questions, answered from the twin
five.para: It can read the sender's orders and propose, not pay. A trace and a decision record show what happened. A pause, routing above $200 and a person intervene. The expected amount and a nightly reconciliation verify. And whoever owns the risk decides on more autonomy, from the record.

evidence.line: The evidence is the case record, and who signed
evidence.para: Precedents that held, decided first by a person with reasons, are the evidence for removing the human; a case that differs is distinguished and goes back. Accountability sits with whoever signed off the policy at that altitude. Ask a team for both: show me the cases, and show me who signed.

next.line: Where next: the tour, the twin, the series
next.para: The tour walks the vault case by case; the twin can be played on its page or opened full screen; and the four-part series on decision policies is what this builds on.

limits.line: A simulation with assumed minutes and our mapping
limits.para: The twin uses synthetic orders and scripted mistakes, with no model called, so it shows how controls interact, not how often agents err. The minutes are assumptions. Northstar and its numbers are his; the other twelve cases and the grid are ours.

sources.line: His article, his references, and the twin
sources.para: Ashish Rajan's article of 16 October 2026 and his LinkedIn post; the Anthropic, OpenAI and Rabanser references he cites, checked; and the twin, built by this site's agent, every number from its engine.
